newsitem.title: UK: Turkmenistan sees 97 GDP growth, inflation fall.
newsitem.headline: Turkmenistan sees 97 GDP growth, inflation fall.

text.p: Gas-rich Turkmenistan's economy will show real growth of four percent this year while annual inflation will fall to around 25 percent, cental bank chief Hudaiberdu Orazov said on Tuesday.

He said during the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development that the Central Asian state had agreed an economic programme for the year with the International Monetary Fund, including further steps to curb inflation.
"The further strategy foresees real growth of gross domestic product of up to four percent," Orazov said.
The former Soviet republic's GDP fell an estimated four percent in 1996 after a 10 percent fall the previous year, according to data made available at the meeting.
Orazov said the plan worked out with the IMF foresaw inflation of 180 percent this year after 446 percent in 1995 but the actual performance for the year would be better.
"By our calculations, we can bring the annual rate of inflation down to 25-27 percent this year," he said.
Turkmenistan has targeted 1997 natural gas output of 53 billion cubic metres (bcm), up from 35 billion last year, though Orazov said this would depend on consumers' ability to pay.
Under a 1996 deal with Russian gas monopoly Gazprom, Turkmenistan aims to export 20 bcm to European markets.

The desert nation is totally dependent on Russian pipelines to export its gas and its hard currency reserves shrank in 1993 when Moscow diverted its gas to cash-strapped former Soviet republics such as Ukraine.
An export pipeline to Iran is due to go into operation this year and a route through Afghanistan and Pakistan is planned.
Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov decreed a 1,000-day economic plan last week, including privatisation of large enterprises.
The oil and gas sector will not be included in the programme. Telecommunications would also not be subject of an immediate sell-off.
"In the telecommunications sector, we will have privatisation but this will not occur before the end of 1997 or the beginning of 1998."
